newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: DLOUHY SAYS NO NEED FOR CROWN DEVALUATION.
newsitem.headline: DLOUHY SAYS NO NEED FOR CROWN DEVALUATION.

text.p: Czech Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy said on Monday there was no need to devalue the crown to curb ballooning current account and trade deficits but the situation should be monitored closely.
Asked whether he thought the record 100.9 billion crown trade deficit and current account shortfall of 1.7 billion required a change to the exchange rate, Dlouhy told a news conference:
"The current situation does not require it. (But) the current account deficit is approaching the point where it is necessary to observe it quite closely."
The Czech trade deficit hit 100.9 billion crowns for the first eight months of the year, compared with a 59.5 billion crown deficit for the same period in 1995.

The Czech Statistical Bureau has forecast the current account deficit to rise to 81 billion crowns, or 5.7 pct of GDP, in 1996. So far, the trade deficit has not translated into significant pressure on the crown which is supported by large inflows of short-term capital.
Some analysts have said that a devaluation may be needed to keep Czech exports competitively priced.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus had called a meeting for October 8 with his three top economic ministers, central bank governor Josef Tosovsky, and Czech Statistical Bureau director Edvard Outrata to address the situation.
But on Monday Dlouhy said the meeting had been postponed because of a parliamentary session, which could include discussion of the budget. No new date for the meeting has been set.

In September, Dlouhy said the trade deficit could reach crisis proportions in 1997 if current trend continues and called for domestic wage restraint and company restructuring to boost competitiveness.

On Monday, he added that the spiralling deficit was partly attributable to the economic slowdown in the European Union. "If the rate of growth of exports to the European Union had been the same this year as last year, the deficit would be around 25 billion crowns lower," he said.
